nameStory: This hermit crab earned its "long-claw" name from its notably elongated claws, especially compared to other hermit crabs you'll find scuttling around New England tide pools. The scientific name Pagurus longicarpus literally means "long wrist," referring to the extended segments of its claws that make it look like it's wearing oversized gloves.
description: The Long-claw Hermit Crab is a small, active crustacean that makes its home in empty snail shells along our Atlantic coastline. Like all hermit crabs, it has a soft, vulnerable abdomen that it protects by backing into discarded shells, carrying its mobile home wherever it goes. These little crabs are typically about an inch long and have a reddish-brown to olive-green coloration with distinctive long, slender claws. You'll often see them dragging their borrowed shells across sandy bottoms and rocky crevices in shallow coastal waters.

idTips.label: Long, slender claws
idTips.description: The claws are noticeably elongated and thin compared to other hermit crabs, with the right claw usually larger than the left. They feel smooth when gently touched and are often a darker reddish-brown color.

idTips.label: Shell selection
idTips.description: Commonly found in periwinkle, moon snail, and whelk shells. The crab's body fits snugly inside, with only its claws, legs, and eyestalks visible from the opening.

idTips.label: Walking legs
idTips.description: The visible walking legs are banded with reddish-brown and cream colors, creating a striped appearance. They feel smooth and hard to the touch.

idTips.label: Eyestalks
idTips.description: Two mobile eyestalks that can retract quickly when threatened. The eyes appear as small dark dots and move independently to scan for danger.

idTips.label: Active behavior
idTips.description: Constantly on the move, dragging their shells across surfaces with a characteristic scratching sound on hard surfaces. They're quick to retreat into their shells when disturbed.

habitat: Long-claw Hermit Crabs thrive in shallow coastal waters throughout New England, from Maine to Connecticut. You'll find them in tide pools, sandy shallows, eelgrass beds, and around rocky shores where empty snail shells are plentiful. They prefer areas with gentle currents and are often abundant in protected bays, estuaries, and the calmer waters behind barrier beaches.

seasonality.spring: Hermit crabs become more active as waters warm, moving into shallower areas where they're easier to spot. Look for them in tide pools during spring low tides.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most visible and active. This is the best time to observe their shell-swapping behavior and see them in large numbers in shallow, warm waters.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to slightly deeper waters. Shell competition intensifies as crabs prepare for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Much less active and found in deeper waters or buried in sediment. Rarely seen in accessible tide pools during this season.

funFact: When a Long-claw Hermit Crab outgrows its shell, it will actually line up with other hermit crabs in a "housing chain" organized by size, where each crab upgrades to the next larger shell in a synchronized musical-chairs-style swap that can involve a dozen crabs at once!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Flat-clawed Hermit Crab, but the Long-claw's claws are noticeably thinner and more elongated. Memory trick: "Long-claw has long, narrow claws like tweezers; Flat-claw has wide, flat claws like spatulas."
compareHints: Among New England's hermit crabs, the Long-claw is distinguished by its notably slender, elongated claws compared to the Flat-clawed Hermit Crab's broad, flattened pincers. The Acadian Hermit Crab is typically larger and found in deeper, colder waters, while the Long-claw prefers warmer, shallower coastal areas. The Long-claw's banded leg coloration is also more pronounced than its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's hermit crabs, the flat-clawed hermit is unmistakable due to its shield-like claws - the long-claw hermit has thin, extended claws, while the Acadian hermit has more typical rounded pincers.
Compared to its close relative the Long-claw Hermit Crab, the Acadian hermit has a more robust build and prefers colder waters further north.
Among New England's hermit crabs, the hairy hermit is the only one with distinctly fuzzy, bristled legs - its relatives like the Long-claw and Flat-clawed hermit crabs have smooth legs and claws.

Unlike its relatives the Long-claw Hermit (which has elongated claws) and Flat-clawed Hermit (which has flattened, broad claws), the Brown Banded Hermit has proportionally normal-sized claws but sports those unmistakable brown leg bands.
